title: The top African cities in 2026
gist: Oxford Economics' 2026 Global Cities Index ranks Cairo as Africa's top city (255th) and names Accra, Cairo, Dakar, Luanda and Nairobi as 'Cities to Watch', projected to generate one-third of African city GDP growth over 25 years. Human capital and a 213mn urban population boom are Africa's key strengths, but weak governance, fiscal constraints and climate pressures risk the demographic surge undermining rather than lifting city performance. (Byline in text is Michael Becker; raw author field lists Sally Li.)

insights.claim: Cairo is Africa's highest-ranked city in Oxford Economics' 2026 Global Cities Index at 255th globally, with Africa's largest urban economy and a population of 30mn.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Cairo is the default entry point for exposure to Africa's largest urban consumer and services market.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics expects Cairo to add 10mn people over the next 25 years, one of the largest urban population expansions in the world, making its position as Africa's top city unlikely to be dislodged.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Long-duration demand for Cairo housing, utilities, transport and consumer goods looks structurally supported.

insights.claim: Egypt's $58bn New Capital east of Cairo could support growth and improve quality of life by reducing congestion, containing housing costs and modernising infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Watch New Capital execution as a swing factor for Cairo's quality-of-life score and for Egyptian construction/real-estate names.
insights.locator: Located at a strategic crossroads between Africa

insights.claim: Accra (Ghana) and Nairobi (Kenya) rank as Africa's second- and fourth-placed cities in the 2026 Global Cities Index (302nd and 327th globally), driven by growth in ICT and finance sectors that position them as gateways to Africa's consumer economy.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Accra and Nairobi are the leading hubs for African fintech/ICT investment theses.

insights.claim: Accra's ICT sector has grown by almost 19% per year since 2014, part of more than a decade of rapid growth in knowledge sectors.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Sustained ~19% annual ICT growth signals a durable tech-services cluster in Ghana worth tracking for VC and telecom exposure.

insights.claim: Nairobi is set to record the 12th-largest increase in industrial jobs of any city in the world, driven by manufacturing employment gains, as Asian cities moving up the value chain vacate lower-value manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Asian upgrading to advanced manufacturing creates a supply-chain relocation opportunity that Kenya is positioned to capture.
insights.quote: As Asian cities move their industrial production up the value chain towards advanced manufacturing and high-tech goods, they leave space in lower-value manufacturing.

insights.claim: Dakar (Senegal) is an Oxford Economics 'City to Watch' due to strong professional services growth, its strategic westernmost location in Africa, and educational reform to raise skill levels that should deepen its labour market and export potential.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Dakar is a West African services and export-hub play conditional on education reform delivering skills.
insights.locator: These rapid changes explain why these five cities

insights.claim: Luanda (Angola) is leveraging hydrocarbon revenue to fund infrastructure and diversify its economy, with the Port of Luanda aiming to sit at the heart of a southern Atlantic logistics network.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Luanda's diversification story is tied to oil revenues, so oil prices drive its infrastructure investment capacity.
insights.locator: Luanda, by contrast, is more a story

insights.claim: Outside the standout cities, Africa's top 10 in the 2026 Global Cities Index broadly tracks economic development: Port Louis (305th), Algiers (359th), Casablanca (384th), Johannesburg (392nd), Windhoek (411th), Rabat (445th) and Gaborone (449th).
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: City rankings largely mirror national development levels, so ranking upside comes from development catch-up.
insights.locator: Beyond these standouts, the rest of Africa’s top 10

insights.claim: Johannesburg and Windhoek would rank higher in the Global Cities Index but for weak Quality of Life scores, despite strong human capital and environment scores respectively.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Quality-of-life deficits (safety, services) are the binding constraint on Southern African city competitiveness.
insights.locator: Beyond these standouts, the rest of Africa’s top 10

insights.claim: Human Capital is African cities' strongest Global Cities Index category: five rank in the global top 50, with Johannesburg 25th, Nairobi 26th, Kampala 41st, Cairo 42nd and Lagos 50th, and this helped 97 of Africa's 113 indexed cities move up the rankings in 2026.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Africa's comparative advantage is labour and talent, favouring labour-intensive and services offshoring theses.
insights.locator: Human capital is the continent’s key strength

insights.claim: Oxford Economics projects major African cities will add 213mn residents over the next 25 years, about 70% of it working-age, which is 200mn more than Europe's major cities are expected to add.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Africa's urban workforce expansion contrasts with ageing advanced economies and underpins long-run consumer and labour-cost arbitrage themes.
insights.locator: A key driver of this is Africa’s demographic momentum

insights.claim: By 2050 Cairo and Kinshasa will become the world's fourth- and fifth-most-populous cities, Lagos and Luanda will enter the global top 20, and seven more African cities will become megacities (over 10mn people).
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A new generation of African megacities implies huge infrastructure, housing and consumer-market build-outs.
insights.locator: This labour market and population expansion

insights.claim: Africa's 12 megacities are expected to account for more than 20% of global urban population growth over the next 25 years.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A fifth of global urban growth concentrated in a dozen African cities makes them central to any global urbanisation allocation.
insights.locator: This labour market and population expansion

insights.claim: Africa's rapid population growth could undermine rather than lift its cities' performance, because weak governance, climate pressures and fiscal constraints risk producing urbanisation with weak infrastructure, low-value jobs and poor service access; Africa has historically failed to convert demographic strength into economic performance.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: The demographic dividend is not automatic; investors should screen for governance and fiscal capacity rather than population growth alone.
insights.quote: the massive increase in population could actually undermine the performance of African cities
insights.locator: But this rapid growth in the continent’s population

insights.claim: Oxford Economics projects that Cairo, Accra, Nairobi, Dakar and Luanda together will generate one-third of all GDP growth among African cities in the Global Cities Index over the next 25 years, signalling increasing concentration of growth.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Concentrate African urban exposure in these five cities; growth outside them is likely to be thinner.
insights.locator: GDP growth is becoming concentrated in a subset of cities

insights.claim: Converting Africa's youthful population boom into sustainable development will be hard given weak investment, deep poverty and high crime rates across the continent.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Expect wide dispersion in outcomes across African cities; weak investment and crime are key risks to monitor.
insights.quote: that won’t be easy in a continent grappling with weak investment, deep poverty, and high crime rates
insights.locator: Overall, Africa is a rapidly changing continent
